answer.exemplar: Once the margins are fixed the counts are not four free numbers, because the last row is whatever is left after the other rows and the last column is whatever is left after the other columns, so one of the four cells is pinned by the other three and the statistic is free to move along a single dimension. In a table with more rows and columns the same pinning repeats, which is why the count works out to rows minus one times columns minus one, and a 2 by 2 table always has exactly one degree of freedom whatever its counts happen to be. Treating all four cells as independent would let a table contradict its own totals, and treating seven of twelve as free in a 4 by 3 table would count cells the margins already determine.

questions.explanation: A strong response notes that the last row and the last column are determined by the others once the totals are fixed, applies that to the 2 by 2 table by showing only one cell can move freely, extends it to the general case as rows minus one times columns minus one, and explains that counting more cells as free would let a table contradict the margins it was built from.
questions.hint: Ask how many of the four cells you can change without altering any total.
questions.learningObjective: derive the degrees of freedom of a table from its margins

answer.exemplar: The design puts 5 of the 10 improved volunteers in each group, so every cell has an expected count of 5, and the statistic of 12.80 on 1 degree of freedom is far past the 3.84 that the 5 percent level requires, so improvement and group really are linked in these 20 volunteers and the trial deserves a follow-up. What the result does not do is pick a direction of cause, since nobody was told which group they were in, and it does not promise the same split in a fresh trial, since a 20-volunteer study is a small sample even when every expected count is comfortably above five. Treating p below 0.001 as certainty also misreads what was tested, because the claim on trial was a statement about improvement and group jointly, with no mechanism named.

questions.explanation: A strong response reports that all four expected counts are 5 so the approximation is safe here, reads 12.80 on 1 degree of freedom as clearing the 3.84 cut-off and therefore showing a real association between improvement and group, and then separates that from what the test cannot settle, namely any direction of cause, whether the split repeats in a new trial, and any claim that a p value below 0.001 is certainty rather than a statement about this one sample.
questions.hint: Ask what the design put in each cell before trusting the cut-off at all.
